items.title: Only 1.5 percent of human DNA codes for proteins
items.claim: The human genome has about 3 billion base pairs. Of these, only about 1.5 percent — 45 million bases — encode proteins. The rest was once called 'junk DNA'. Most of it isn't.
items.prompt: What does the non-coding majority actually do?

options.text: It's all junk left over from evolution

It includes promoters, enhancers, insulators, microRNA genes, long non-coding RNAs, ribosomal RNA, structural sequences, transposable elements (some still active), and regions whose function is still being mapped
It codes for proteins we haven't found
It's only present in cells that have stopped dividing

items.reveal_title: ENCODE and the redefinition of junk
items.reveal:
The ENCODE Project (2012) reported biochemical activity (transcription, transcription-factor binding, chromatin features) in about 80 percent of the genome. Whether all of this counts as 'function' was hotly debated.

Certain categories of non-coding DNA have clear roles:
- Promoters/enhancers: regulate gene expression in time and place. Disrupting them causes disease (e.g., enhancer mutations causing limb deformity).
- microRNAs: ~22-nucleotide RNAs that tune protein levels.
- Long non-coding RNAs: XIST silences a whole X chromosome in females.
- Transposable elements: about 45 percent of the genome; some still mobile.

Much DNA may also be 'spacer' or accumulated parasitic sequence with no current function — but the cell is full of layers of regulation built from non-coding DNA.
items.why: Genome size was thought to scale with organism complexity. Onions have 5 times more DNA than humans. Most DNA isn't there to encode proteins — and may be doing many things at once.

items.title: A woman who died in 1951 still has dividing cells today
items.claim: Normal human cells divide about 50 times and then stop (the Hayflick limit). HeLa cells, taken from Henrietta Lacks's cervical tumour in 1951, divide indefinitely. They are in laboratories on every continent.

options.text: Constitutive expression of telomerase — the enzyme that rebuilds telomeres on chromosome ends — allows them to divide without losing telomeric DNA, bypassing the Hayflick limit. The HPV-derived oncogenes E6 and E7 also disable normal tumour suppressors
Special preservation chemicals keep them alive
All cancer cells are technically immortal

items.reveal_title: Telomeres, telomerase, and the loophole around cell senescence
items.reveal:
Linear chromosomes lose a small amount of DNA from their ends with each replication (the 'end replication problem'). Once telomeres reach a critical short length, cells trigger senescence — the Hayflick limit, named after Leonard Hayflick (1961).

Most adult cells suppress telomerase. Germline cells, stem cells and most cancers reactivate it. HeLa cells express telomerase robustly. Combined with disabled tumour suppressors (p53 and Rb, neutralised by HPV-18 oncoproteins), they grow without limit.

HeLa cells were the first immortal human cell line. They were taken without Henrietta Lacks's consent. The ethical legacy is still being addressed — her family didn't learn the cells existed until 1973, and only signed an agreement with the NIH on access to her genome in 2013.
items.why: Cell death is taught as inevitable. The cellular machinery to bypass it exists; cancer cells exploit it; HeLa cells made it visible.

items.title: A tumour is a tiny evolving ecosystem
items.claim: Cancer cells accumulate mutations. Cells with mutations that confer growth advantages dominate. Drug treatment kills the susceptible cells but spares resistant ones — which then dominate the regrown tumour.
items.prompt: Why is cancer so hard to cure even with effective drugs?

options.text: Drugs don't work on cancer cells

A tumour contains millions to billions of slightly genetically different cells; selection pressure from a drug acts on the existing variation and rapidly enriches resistant clones — the same evolutionary process as antibiotic resistance, but inside a single patient

items.reveal_title: Tumour heterogeneity and the cost of monotherapy
items.reveal:
Single-cell sequencing of tumours reveals enormous clonal diversity. A 5 cm tumour may contain 10 to the 9 cells, each with its own profile of acquired mutations. Subclones can have different drug sensitivities, growth rates and metastatic potentials.

Treating with a single targeted therapy selects for whichever cells are pre-existingly resistant. Within months, the tumour regrows — now dominated by the resistant subclone. Combination therapy (targeting multiple pathways at once) makes resistance much less likely, by analogy with HIV's HAART protocol.

The Peter Nowell paper (1976) first proposed clonal evolution in cancer. Recent decades have made it the dominant framework, with implications for drug strategy, biomarker design, and the inevitability of resistance.
items.why: Cancer is taught as one disease. It's an evolving population of cells subject to selection — making it as much an ecological and evolutionary problem as a medical one.
